nameStory: The 'passion' in passionflower comes from Spanish missionaries who saw religious symbolism in the intricate blooms - the crown-like center representing Christ's crown of thorns, and the prominent stamens symbolizing the nails of the crucifixion. The name 'maypop' comes from the satisfying 'pop' sound the ripe fruits make when you step on them, though they actually ripen later in summer than May!
description: Purple passionflower is a fast-growing perennial vine that climbs or trails along the ground with twining tendrils. It produces some of the most spectacular and complex flowers you'll ever see - intricate purple and white blooms that look almost alien with their prominent crown of frilly filaments. The vine can spread extensively through underground runners, and in late summer produces egg-shaped yellowish fruits about the size of a chicken egg. This is one of the hardiest members of the tropical passionflower family, though it's quite rare in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Absolutely unmistakable 3-4 inch wide flowers with five white petals topped by a crown of purple and white frilly filaments that feel soft to touch, plus five prominent stamens and three purple styles rising from the center like tiny clubs

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-lobed leaves that feel smooth and slightly waxy, each lobe pointed and roughly equal in size, arranged alternately along the stem with a distinctive sweet, grassy smell when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Fast-growing vine that climbs using curly tendrils that spiral tightly around supports, or trails along the ground forming dense mats that can spread several feet in a season

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Oval yellowish-green fruits about 2-3 inches long that feel firm when ripe and contain a sweet, jelly-like pulp with many small dark seeds that rattle when shaken

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth green stems that feel sturdy but flexible, with small thread-like tendrils emerging near each leaf that actively curl and twist when touched

habitat: In New England, purple passionflower is extremely rare and likely represents garden escapes or plantings rather than truly wild populations. When found, look for it in sunny, well-drained areas like field edges, fence rows, or disturbed sites with sandy or loamy soil. It needs protection from harsh winter winds and may not survive the coldest New England winters without some shelter.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the root system in late spring, with the distinctive three-lobed leaves appearing first as the vine begins its rapid growth phase.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in mid to late summer with the spectacular flowers opening in the morning and lasting just one day each, though new flowers continue opening for weeks. This is when the plant is most easily identified.
seasonality.fall: Yellowish egg-shaped fruits ripen in early fall and the foliage begins to yellow. The vine may continue blooming until the first frost in warmer locations.
seasonality.winter: The above-ground portions die back completely to the ground, leaving no trace of the plant until spring growth emerges from the persistent root system.

funFact: Each purple passionflower bloom lives for exactly one day - opening in the morning with an almost audible 'pop' as the frilly crown unfurls, then closing forever by evening, but the plant keeps this daily flower show going for months by producing new buds continuously!
confusionNotes: With only 2 recorded observations in New England, you're unlikely to confuse this with anything else because those spectacular flowers are absolutely unique - no other vine in our region produces anything even remotely similar to these intricate purple and white crowns.
contextualKnowledge: While called 'maypop,' the fruits actually ripen in late summer, not May. This southern species is at the very northern edge of its range in New England, so most sightings here are likely cultivated plants that have spread from gardens rather than truly wild populations.
compareHints: Purple passionflower is the only member of the Passiflora genus recorded in New England, making it unique among our native and naturalized vines. The closest you might come to similar complexity in flower structure would be some of the wild orchids, but those grow as terrestrial herbs rather than climbing vines. No other vine in our region produces anything approaching the intricate, layered flower structure of the passionflowers.
